Tea with the neighbours

Sunday afternoon, in the second week of the visit, in the living room in Cotroceni. Mrs Fumiko has prepared tea for the neighbours: Mrs Doina has come, and Mr Petre from the floor above (the owner of the dog that barked at night in September), plus Elena, Mihai’s mother. A few days earlier, Mihai took the sisters to grandpa Gheorghe’s village. Doina talks to Ana in Spanish and Mihai translates the rest; the Romanians’ lines are written in simple Japanese.
Thank you all for coming. Please, have some tea from Kyoto.
For Ana I’ve made hōjicha, which has little caffeine.
Oh, what a beautiful green! …Oh, it’s bitter! But what a lovely aroma.
At first it’s bitter, isn’t it? But the more you drink, the more you notice its sweetness.
(In Romanian) It’s true. The second sip isn’t as bitter as the first.
Mr Petre says the second sip isn’t as bitter as the first.
There’s nobody in the world who makes tea as well as Fumiko.
Sister, you’re praising me too much. …Mr Petre, would you like another cup?
(Embarrassed) Thank you, I’d love one. …Mihai, I’m sorry my dog barked at night in the autumn.
(Laughing) It’s fine now. Although back then it was so bad that I couldn’t sleep.
Ana, how was it in the village? Mihai took the two ladies there, didn’t he?
I couldn’t go. Although the more I was told “no”, the more I wanted to go.
The mountain road is long. As a doctor, I can’t allow that.
(In Romanian) Instead, I stayed with Ana the whole time.
The village was wonderful. The snowy mountains, the wooden house and grandpa’s smile.
The more I remember it, the more I want to go back.
And Bucharest? It’s colder than Madrid, isn’t it?
Yes, it’s cold. But this city: the more I see of it, the more I love it.
(Wiping her tears) Oh my. I’m so happy that tears are coming to my eyes.
Mrs Doina, I’ll give you a little of this tea, so you can drink it again.
Thank you! But even if I make it, it won’t turn out as good as Mrs Fumiko’s.
The more often you make it, the better you get. It took me fifty years too.
Fifty years…! Then I’ll start today.

no-me-ba no-mu ho-do: the verb is said twice, first with ば, then plain. Make a small pause after ほど, before the second part: “the more you drink… / the more…”.
ho-do: short “o”, as in “hot”. hoo-ji-cha: long “hō”, as long as two syllables. Length matters: ほど (as much as), ほう (direction, side).
ni-ga-i: three syllables; many Japanese speakers soften the “g” and nasalise it slightly (almost “nga”). In the negative: ni-ga-ku na-i.
1. ～ば ～ほど: “the more…, the more…”

You learned the ～ば form in chapter 24 (if…). Now you use it in a new pattern: say the same word twice, first in the ～ば form, then in the dictionary form, and add ほど. Literally: “if you drink, as much as you drink, …” → “the more you drink, the more…”. The second part says what changes.
group 1 verb
The more you drink, the better it is.
group 2 verb
The more you see it, the more you love it.
irregular verb
The more you practise, the better you get.
The longer you wait, the happier you are.
The quieter the room, the better.
With Sino-Japanese verbs that take する you can repeat just する: れんしゅう すれば する ほど (no need to repeat れんしゅう). With な-adjectives you can also say しずか で あれば ある ほど, which is more formal.
Don’t forget: いい → よければ よい ほど (not “いければ”). E.g. てんき は よければ よい ほど いい (the better the weather, the better). And the second part can’t be a request or an order: it states a change or a fact.

English does exactly the same with “the more… the more…”, except that we use the comparative (“more”, “better”). Japanese doesn’t need a “more”: the change is understood from なる (“becomes”) or from context.
2. The short version, and ～ば ～ほど with the passive and with ～たい
In everyday speech the ～ば part can be dropped: のむ ほど おいしく なる means the same as のめば のむ ほど おいしく なる. The short version is easier, but the double one sounds more expressive.
The older you get, the more often you remember the past.
The more you’re told “no”, the more you want to go. (the passive, ch. 31)
The higher we climbed the mountain, the whiter the landscape became.
Any form that has a ～ば can go into the pattern: the passive (いわれれば いわれる ほど), the causative (れんしゅう させれば させる ほど), the negative (ねなければ ねない ほど つかれる = the less you sleep, the more tired you are).
3. A は B ほど ～ない: “A isn’t as… as B”

In chapter 12 you compared with より: A は B より ～ (A is more… than B). For a negative comparison Japanese uses ほど: A は B ほど ～ない = “A isn’t as… as B”. The meaning is the same as “B is more… than A”, but said more gently, from A’s side.
With より (affirmative)
With ほど (negative)
The second sip isn’t as bitter as the first.
Bucharest isn’t as warm as Madrid.
My tea isn’t as good as Mrs Fumiko’s.
In this sense ほど needs a NEGATIVE. ✗ ブカレスト は マドリード ほど さむい. For the affirmative you use より: ブカレスト は マドリード より さむい. It also works with verbs: きのう ほど ふって いない (it isn’t snowing as hard as yesterday).
English has the pair “more… than” / “not as… as”. Japanese has the same pair: より / ほど～ない. Think of ほど as “up to B’s level”: it doesn’t come up to B’s level.
4. B ほど ～ X は いない / ない: “nobody is as… as B”
With ほど you can make an “upside-down” superlative, very common in Japanese: instead of “B is the most…”, you say “there is nobody / nothing as… as B”. For people and animals use いない, for things ない.
Nothing is as important as family.
There’s no greater happiness than being able to see the people you love.
Compared with いちばん (ch. 12): ふみこ が いちばん じょうず だ is a simple statement; ふみこ ほど じょうず な ひと は いない is more emotional, like saying in English “there’s nobody in the world like her”.
5. ～ほど: “so… that…” (degree)
ほど after a verb (usually in the dictionary form or the negative) shows HOW great a state is: “to the point where…”. The part before ほど is a concrete image, the part after it is the state.
Natural English
happy enough for tears to come out
I’m so happy I could cry.
noisy enough that you can’t sleep
It was so noisy I couldn’t sleep.
tired enough to die
I’m dead tired.
it snowed enough that you couldn’t walk
It snowed so much you couldn’t walk anymore.

Sometimes the state is left unsaid: あの とき は、ねむれない ほど でした (back then it was so bad I couldn’t sleep). And after numbers ほど means “about”: いっぷん ほど まつ (you wait about a minute, ch. 38), いちじかん ほど (about an hour). Here ほど is similar to くらい / ぐらい.

English has images of degree too: “dead tired”, “finger-licking good”. Japanese puts them before ほど: ほっぺた が おちる ほど おいしい (literally “so good your cheeks fall off”, i.e. “finger-licking good”) is an expression you’ll hear a lot!

さくらんぼ の き の さじ — The cherry-wood spoon
On the morning they left for the village, Ana stood at the door, pouting.
“I want to go too.” “No. The mountain road takes more than three hours. As a doctor, absolutely not.”
Ana sighed and handed Mrs Suzuki her old notebook. It was the notebook where she had written down grandpa’s stories in the summer.
“Read it in the car. For me.” Elena was going to come and stay with Ana.
Once they had left the city, the road slowly climbed into the mountains.
The higher they went, the whiter the landscape became. Snow had settled on the branches and on the roofs.
In the back seat, Mrs Fumiko was reading aloud from Ana’s notebook.
Little Mihai who spilled the bucket of milk. Grandpa who chased off the bear with pots. The two soldiers who made up thanks to a flute.
“The more I read, the more I can’t wait to meet him,” said Mrs Suzuki, and Mihai smiled sheepishly in the rear-view mirror.
On the way, Mrs Fumiko said, “Mihai, excuse me, could you stop for a moment? I’d like to take a photo of this landscape.”
When they got out of the car, the air was cold and clear. The colder it got, the redder the sisters’ cheeks became.
“Winter in Kyoto is beautiful too, but it isn’t as vast as these mountains,” said Mrs Fumiko.
In front of the wooden house, grandpa was waiting in his best coat. Next to him stood Sura, the horse.
To the two women getting out of the car, grandpa said, in the Japanese Mihai had taught him over the phone: “G-good afternoon.”
And he bowed awkwardly. The sisters bowed even more deeply. Then grandpa bowed even more, more deeply still.
The three of them kept bowing until Mihai stopped them, laughing: “Grandpa, you’ll hurt your back!”
Then grandpa wrapped Mrs Suzuki’s hand in both of his: “Thank you for looking after Mihai in Madrid.”
When Mihai translated, Mrs Suzuki shook her head: “No, he looked after me, not the other way round.”
It was warm in the house, thanks to the stove. On the wall, grandma Ileana’s apron is still hanging there.
Mrs Suzuki looked for a long time, in silence, at the photo of the two soldiers and the flute next to it.
Mrs Fumiko sat down on the little stool by the stove. “That’s the stool I made for Mihai when he was a boy,” grandpa laughed.
“Nobody has sat on this stool as long as Mihai.”
After a while, three old women from the village came with pies and cozonac. The news that “guests from Japan have come” had already spread through the whole village.
Mrs Fumiko asked Mihai: “May I boil some water on the stove? I’d like to offer everyone tea.”
After the first sip of green tea, the old women looked at each other: “Bitter!”
But drunk with the sweet cozonac, they all said “oh, it’s good” and asked for another cup.
The youngest of the old women asked, through Mihai: “Would you teach me how to make it too?”
Mrs Fumiko happily showed her how to pour a little at a time, in turn, and that the last drop is the best.
Grandpa held his cup in both hands and said quietly: “Ileana often made linden tea for everyone too. How many years has it been since anyone made tea in this house?”
In the evening, in front of the stove, grandpa listened to the sisters’ story. How they hadn’t spoken for fifty years. The letter Mihai had carried.
“We wasted so much time,” said Mrs Suzuki, and grandpa shook his head.
“It wasn’t wasted. The longer you’ve waited, the greater the joy when you meet again. When you’ve lived as long as I have, you understand that.”
“The people you love, you must see while you still can. Nothing is more important than that.”
While Mihai translated, the sisters held hands in silence.
That night it snowed quietly outside. “Night in the mountains is even quieter than in Kyoto,” whispered Mrs Fumiko.
That night, until late, the light was on in grandpa’s workshop.
The next morning, grandpa gave Mrs Fumiko a small wooden spoon. It was a tea spoon, carved from the cherry tree in the yard.
“For a person from the land of cherry blossoms, a spoon of cherry wood.”
Mrs Fumiko hugged the spoon to her chest and laughed until tears came. “I’ll use it with great care at the teahouse.”
After breakfast, Mrs Suzuki gave Sura an apple.
The more Sura ate, the more it seemed to want, and it pushed its muzzle into Mrs Suzuki’s shoulder. “Oh, just like Tama.”
When they said goodbye, grandpa said: “Next time come all of you, and show me my great-granddaughter’s face.” The sisters answered “without fail” and bowed deeply.
Grandpa and Sura stood at the gate until the car taking them home could no longer be seen.
All the way back, Mrs Fumiko held the little spoon tightly in her hand.
When they got to Bucharest, Ana came running to the door. “How was it? Tell me everything!”
Mrs Suzuki laughed as she took off her coat. “The more I tell, the longer it gets. Let’s make some tea first, then we’ll take our time.”
